tldr: An Oct 27 arXiv paper framed edge MoE inference as an expert-weight movement problem rather than a compute problem. Two Hacker News posts followed within a week, showing the same memory constraint being attacked on a single DGX Spark and on Macs.
whats_new: A Show HN project (Nov 3) claims faster MoE inference on a Mac with less RAM, following a Nov 2 post on running a 124B MoE on one DGX Spark.
why_it_matters: MoE models only fit small hardware if expert weights are moved or compressed cleverly, so memory footprint, not FLOPs, decides which models you can serve locally.

status.detail: Research and hobbyist projects converge on memory-bound MoE inference on small hardware.

beats.headline: CRISP: pruning plus scheduling for edge MoE
beats.summary: Names expert-weight movement, not compute, as the edge bottleneck.

beats.headline: 124B MoE tuned on a single DGX Spark
Show HN: faster MoE on Mac with less RAM

open_questions: Do the Mac and DGX Spark projects publish tokens-per-second and RAM figures that others can reproduce?
Do practitioner projects adopt expert pruning or scheduling ideas like CRISP's?
take_for_builders: If you plan local MoE serving, benchmark peak memory and expert-load traffic on your target hardware before trusting parameter-count estimates.
